question: What is the main job of muscle tissue in the human body?

options.A: To produce force and cause movement
options.B: To insulate internal organs from extreme heat
options.C: To provide structural support for epithelial sheets
options.D: To filter metabolic wastes from the bloodstream

explanation: Muscle tissue is specialized to contract, generate force, and make movement possible throughout the body. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h1)

question: What is another common name for an individual muscle cell?
explanation: Because individual muscle cells are long and thread-like, they are commonly called muscle fibers. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h1)

question: What distinct feature can you see when looking at skeletal muscle tissue under a microscope?

options.A: Hollow tubular structures filled with cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Spindle-shaped cells lacking any visible bands
options.C: Branching networks with dark intercalated discs

explanation: Skeletal muscle fibers have a regular arrangement of proteins that show up under a microscope as distinct light and dark bands, known as striations. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h2)

question: Why do skeletal muscle fibers have more than one nucleus?

options.A: To allow the cell to survive if a single nucleus is damaged by lactic acid
options.B: To produce hormones that regulate blood calcium levels during contraction
options.C: Because they divide rapidly by mitosis whenever a muscle is injured
options.D: Because they fuse together from many smaller embryonic cells during development

explanation: During development, many smaller precursor cells join together to form a single long skeletal muscle fiber, leaving all of their nuclei inside the shared cell. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h2)

question: Which specific structure allows electrical signals to pass quickly between neighboring heart muscle cells?
explanation: Intercalated discs contain special channels that connect neighboring heart cells electrically, helping them contract together in unison. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h3)

question: What would happen if intercalated discs stopped working properly in the heart?

options.A: Blood vessels would lose their ability to constrict under stress
options.B: Heart muscle cells would lose their synchronized contraction pattern
options.C: The heart would instantly stop growing larger during childhood
options.D: Skeletal muscles throughout the limbs would become paralyzed

explanation: Without the communication channels in intercalated discs, individual heart cells would contract randomly, ruining the heart's ability to pump blood efficiently. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the typical shape of a smooth muscle cell under a microscope?
explanation: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, meaning they are wider in the middle and narrow down to pointed ends. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h4)

question: During the third stage of labor, which type of muscle in the uterus contracts strongly to push out the placenta and seal off blood vessels?
explanation: The myometrium of the uterus is made of smooth muscle, which provides the involuntary contractions needed during and after childbirth. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which property lets a muscle fiber shorten forcefully when it receives a signal?
explanation: Contractility is the specific ability of muscle tissue to actively shorten and create a pulling force. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h5)

question: How is extensibility different from elasticity in muscle tissue?

options.A: Extensibility is stretching without damage, while elasticity is returning to the original length
options.B: Extensibility occurs only in cardiac muscle, while elasticity is unique to smooth muscle
options.C: Extensibility destroys old protein fibers, while elasticity builds new myofibrils
options.D: Extensibility generates force during movement, while elasticity receives nerve signals

explanation: Extensibility allows a muscle to stretch safely, while elasticity helps it snap back to its normal resting size afterward. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h5)

question: What are the two main protein filaments responsible for muscle contraction?
explanation: Thin actin filaments and thick myosin filaments slide past each other inside the muscle cell to cause shortening and contraction. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why do midwives commonly give oxytocin during the third stage of labor?

options.A: To improve electrical conductivity across cardiac intercalated discs
options.B: To stimulate smooth muscle contraction in the myometrium and prevent excessive bleeding
options.C: To increase the extensibility of abdominal wall connective tissues
options.D: To relax skeletal muscle fibers in the pelvic floor and widen the birth canal

explanation: Oxytocin targets receptors on the smooth muscle of the uterus, making it contract firmly to clamp down on open blood vessels after delivery. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical clinical concern related to muscle tissue dysfunction in maternity care?

options.A: Uterine inertia failing to progress active labor
options.B: Primary visual cortex degradation causing sudden blindness
options.C: Postpartum hemorrhage due to poor myometrial tone
options.D: Muscle tetany resulting from severe maternal hypocalcemia

explanation: Visual problems involve nervous tissue in the brain, whereas uterine inertia, postpartum hemorrhage, and tetany are clinical concerns directly tied to muscle function. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T8#BMP111_U1_T8_h7)
